sit_018:n1.prompt:
You are helping me scope a possible hijack of my domain and/or social accounts during the first hour of an incident. Your job is to gather evidence and prepare a triage sheet. Deciding what fell first is my call.

First, ask me for anything missing: my domain(s), my registrar, my email provider, the affected social handles, and any known-good DNS records I have (a zone export, screenshot, or notes). Use your configured credentials only for read-only access. Do not change any settings, passwords, or records.

Then:
1. Look up the domain's current registration state via public RDAP. Record the registrar of record, status codes (for example, whether a transfer lock is present or missing), nameservers, and last-updated date. Flag any registrar or nameserver I don't recognize.
2. Query current public DNS: nameservers, MX, SPF/DKIM/DMARC TXT records, and A/AAAA/CNAME records for the main site and mail hosts. Compare each against my known-good records and mark every difference. Treat changed MX records or nameservers as top priority, because that is how one stolen login becomes all of them.
3. Where you have read access, list recent sign-ins, new devices, mail forwarding rules, recovery email or phone changes, and security alerts for the registrar account, the email account, and each social handle. Note timestamps and locations.
4. Build a single timeline of suspicious events across all accounts, oldest first.

Done looks like a one-page triage sheet with:
- A table per asset (registrar, DNS, email, each social handle) showing a status of appears intact, changed, or unknown, plus the evidence behind it.
- The combined timeline.
- Open questions only I can answer (for example, "Did you add this forwarding rule?").

Do not label which account was the entry point. List the candidates with their supporting evidence instead.

Report back with that sheet, then stop for human sign-off before anything further happens.

sit_018:n2.prompt:
You are helping me contain a suspected hijack of my domain and related accounts. This step locks down everything I still control before the attacker spreads further. My registrar is {{vendor}}. Use your configured credentials for its API or dashboard.

First, ask me for anything missing:
- the affected domain(s)
- my known-good DNS and MX records from before the incident (a zone export, config file, or screenshot)
- the accounts tied to the domain: registrar, email provider, social handles, and DNS host if separate

Then:
1. In {{vendor}}, review account security. Check whether 2FA is on and whether it uses a hardware security key. List all API credentials with their scopes and any IP allowlisting. List every account user and contact. Flag anything I don't recognize, but don't delete anything without asking me.
2. Enable the transfer lock on every affected domain. Report whether a registry-lock option is available for the critical ones.
3. Pull the current DNS records through {{vendor}}'s DNS API and compare them with my known-good set. Pay special attention to MX, NS, SPF/DKIM/DMARC TXT records, CNAMEs, and any new subdomains. Show me the differences and your proposed corrections. Apply each correction only after I approve it.
4. Write a prioritized lockdown checklist for me to do myself:
   - rotate passwords, starting with email, then the registrar, then social accounts
   - enroll hardware-key 2FA
   - revoke unknown sessions and connected apps
   - replace any suspicious API credentials with new least-privilege ones
   Credential changes are mine. Do not handle passwords or keys.

Done looks like this: the transfer lock is confirmed on, DNS and MX match known-good (or my approved fixes are applied), and I have a checklist showing each account's status.

Report back with:
- lock status per domain
- the DNS differences and what you changed
- any suspicious users or credentials you found
- any sign that the domain has already been transferred away or the registrar account is lost, which means escalating to the registrar's compromise process

sit_018:n3.prompt:
You are helping me recover a domain that may have been hijacked. Your job is to prepare my registrar compromise case and, if the domain was transferred to another registrar, an ICANN transfer-dispute complaint. Then stop for human sign-off. Speed matters because ICANN's transfer rules include 60-day windows, so work quickly.

If any of these are missing, ask me first: the domain name, my registrar's name, the approximate date I noticed the problem, and whether I still have access to my registrar account.

Steps:
1. Look up the domain's current registration state with a public RDAP lookup. Do not guess. Record the sponsoring registrar, status codes (such as transfer locks), the creation and last-updated dates, and the nameservers. Note whether the sponsoring registrar differs from mine, because that signals an inter-registrar transfer.
2. Build an ownership-evidence checklist and pack. Include the original registration date and receipts, renewal and payment records (invoices, card last four digits), and any prior registration records showing my details or nameservers. Add registrar emails sent to me, DNS history, and a timeline of what changed and when. Flag items only I can supply, such as government ID. I will provide those myself.
3. Draft the registrar compromise case. Give a concise account of the unauthorized access and the timeline. List what was changed (contacts, DNS, MX records, transfer). State the remedy requested: restore my control, re-apply the transfer lock and reverse the changes. Close with a list of attached evidence.
4. If the domain was transferred away, draft an ICANN complaint for https://www.icann.org/compliance/complaint. Describe the unauthorized transfer, with dates measured against the 60-day rules, and name both registrars. Reference the evidence. Note that ICANN typically expects me to have contacted my registrar first.

Done looks like this: an RDAP snapshot, the evidence checklist with gaps flagged, and both drafts ready for my review.

Do not submit, sign or send anything, and do not attest to any facts on my behalf. Report back with the drafts, the checklist and any deadline you identified. Then stop for human sign-off.

sit_018:n4.prompt:
You are helping me respond to a possible hijack of my domain. Your job in this step is narrow: establish the live registration state and transfer timeline from authoritative RDAP data, so we work from facts, not guesses. Do not contact anyone or change anything. This is read-only.

Ask me first if missing:
- The domain name in question.
- The registrar I believe it should be at, and roughly when I last saw it working normally.
- Any registrar or transfer notification emails I received, with dates.

Actions:
1. Look up the domain on ICANN's lookup tool at https://lookup.icann.org/. It queries RDAP. Record the full result. If the tool points to a registrar RDAP server, follow that and capture its response too.
2. Extract and list:
   - Current sponsoring registrar and IANA ID.
   - Registrant and contacts, where not redacted.
   - Status codes (e.g. clientTransferProhibited, serverHold, pendingTransfer, pendingDelete).
   - Nameservers.
   - Creation, expiration, and last-updated dates.
   - Any transfer or registrar-change event dates.
3. Compare against what I told you. Flag any of these:
   - A different registrar than expected.
   - Missing transfer lock.
   - Unfamiliar nameservers.
   - Recent update or transfer dates.
4. Build a timeline: last known good state, then any changes visible in RDAP, then today. Note how many days have passed since any registrar change or transfer. Time limits under ICANN's transfer policy, including 60-day rules, may matter for a dispute.
5. Optionally resolve the domain's current nameservers and MX records via public DNS. Note whether they match what I expect. Mail redirection is how one stolen login spreads.

Done looks like a short report with:
- (a) The raw RDAP fields captured, with lookup timestamp.
- (b) A plain verdict: still at my registrar and locked; at my registrar but altered or unlocked; or transferred away, and to whom.
- (c) The dated timeline with day counts.
- (d) Discrepancies and what they imply for next steps: a registrar compromise case versus an ICANN transfer dispute or complaint.

Mark anything you couldn't confirm as unknown rather than inferring it.

sit_018:n5.prompt:
You are helping me recover a hijacked online account by preparing everything for the platform's own official recovery flow. These flows (Google's hacked-account flow at https://support.google.com/accounts/answer/6294825, Instagram's hacked-account page, and X's recovery process in its help center) deliberately verify that I am the real owner. They may use selfie checks, device history or ID upload. You must not try to pass those checks yourself.

First, ask me for anything missing:
- Which platform(s) and which account handle or email address were taken.
- When I last had access, and from which devices and locations.
- My recovery email and phone number, and whether the attacker changed either one.
- Any security-alert emails I received, such as "password changed" or "new sign-in" notices.
- Whether posts were published or messages and mail were read while the account was compromised.

Then:
1. For each platform, confirm the correct official recovery entry point. For Google, use the URL above. For Instagram and X, find the current flow from their own help centers. Do not use third-party "recovery services."
2. Build a pre-filled answer sheet for each flow. Include account identifiers, my last-known passwords (I will type these myself, so just note that I need them ready), approximate account creation date, frequently used devices, usual sign-in locations, recovery contacts, and a short factual description of what happened and when.
3. Make a checklist of what I should have on hand: the original device and network if possible, a photo ID if the platform asks for it, and access to my recovery email and phone.
4. Draft a short note I can send to affected contacts if posts went out or mail was read.

Then stop for human sign-off. I will run each verification flow myself. Do not submit forms, accept terms, upload ID, or answer verification challenges on my behalf.

Report back with the following:
- The official URL for each platform.
- The completed answer sheet.
- The on-hand checklist.
- The contact-notification draft.
- Any gaps you couldn't fill.

sit_018:n6.prompt:
You are helping me with one step of recovering a hijacked domain or social account. Someone took over my handle or mailbox, and posts may have gone out or mail may have been read. The goal is to tell the affected people quickly and plainly, before screenshots spread. Your job is to prepare everything for that. The telling itself remains a human step: I send every message and make every post myself. Do not send, post, or publish anything on my behalf.

Ask me for anything missing:
- Which accounts were affected (social handle, email mailbox, domain/website) and the approximate compromise window.
- What I know went out: posts, DMs, emails, links, payment or credential requests.
- What may have been exposed: mail read, contacts viewed, files accessed.
- My current status: which accounts I've regained and locked, and what is still in progress.

Then prepare:
1. An exposure list. If you have read access through my configured tools, review the affected window in my sent mail, sent DMs, and post history (use your configured credentials). List who likely received malicious content or whose information may have been read. Flag uncertainty instead of guessing.
2. A short public post for the affected platform. Say what happened, when, what not to click or pay, and that it wasn't me. Make it honest, specific, and free of spin.
3. A direct message/email template for people who were targeted, with a version for anyone whose data may have been read.
4. A brief note for my team or key customers if business accounts or the domain were involved.
5. A list of messages that should be deleted or marked as fraudulent once I have access. Prepare it only; do not delete anything.

Done looks like this: an exposure list, plus ready-to-send drafts with recipients grouped by message type. Report back with the drafts, the recipient groups with counts, any gaps in what you could see, and a recommended sending order, fastest-harm first. Then wait for me.

sit_018:n7.prompt:
You are helping me harden my domain and accounts after recovering them from a hijack. Goal: registrar lock on, hardware security keys as 2FA everywhere they're supported, DNS monitoring running, and all of it documented in one hardening record.

First ask me for anything missing: my domain(s), my registrar, my DNS host, my email provider, the social accounts involved, and how many hardware keys I own (ideally two per person, a primary and a backup).

Then:
1. Registration state: look up my domain on RDAP and record status codes, registrar, nameservers, and expiry. Check whether the transfer-prohibited (registrar lock) status is present. If not, use your configured credentials to enable transfer lock through my registrar's dashboard or API. If my registrar offers a stronger registry lock, note it as an option for me.
2. Account inventory: list every account in the blast radius: registrar, DNS host, email, social handles, and any account whose password reset goes to those. For each, record the current 2FA method, recovery email and phone, and active sessions. Flag SMS-only 2FA and any recovery contact I don't recognize.
3. Hardware keys: for each account that supports security keys, write step-by-step enrollment instructions for both keys, and flag accounts that don't support them. Tapping the physical key is my job. Prepare the checklist and I'll tell you when each is done.
4. DNS monitoring: capture a baseline of current records (A, AAAA, MX, NS, CNAME, TXT including SPF and DMARC). Set up a scheduled check that compares live DNS and RDAP status against the baseline and alerts me on any change, especially MX and NS.
5. Document: write a hardening record with the baseline, lock status, a 2FA matrix, where keys are kept (described only, no secrets), the monitoring schedule, and my registrar's compromise-contact path in case this happens again.

Done means: lock visible on RDAP, every account's 2FA status listed, monitoring active, and the record written. Report back with the record and a short list of remaining gaps.

sit_018:n8.prompt:
You are helping me through a hijacked domain or social account recovery. I've already filed cases: a compromise case with my registrar, possibly an ICANN transfer dispute or complaint, and recovery requests through the platforms' published hacked-account flows (Google, Instagram, X). This step is waiting for those queues to close and checking the domain's registration state on RDAP when they do.

Ask me first for anything missing: the affected domain(s), the registrar's name, every open case or ticket number with its filing date, which platform accounts are in recovery, and the RDAP state I recorded when the incident started.

What to do:
1. Build a case tracker: one row per open case with the owner (registrar, ICANN, or platform), case ID, filing date, last update, and expected next action. Flag any ICANN case where the 60-day transfer rules affect timing.
2. Run an RDAP lookup now for each domain and record the registrar of record, status codes (look for transfer-lock statuses), nameservers, and last-changed dates. Compare against my baseline and call out every difference.
3. Set a polling plan. Re-run the RDAP lookup on a regular cadence I approve, and again whenever I tell you a case has closed. Log each result with a timestamp.
4. When I report a closure, produce a short diff: what RDAP shows now versus before, and whether it matches what the case said would happen. Note any mismatch for me to raise with the registrar or ICANN.

The waiting itself, and any reply to a registrar, ICANN, or platform reviewer, remains a human step. Do not contact case handlers, re-submit recovery forms, or decide on my behalf that a case is resolved. Use your configured credentials only for read-only lookups.

Done looks like this: an up-to-date tracker, a timestamped RDAP log, and a clear note on what changed. Report back with the tracker, the latest RDAP snapshot per domain, any discrepancies, and the date of the next scheduled re-check.
